claims.claim_en: From July 1779 the Spanish blockade squadron under Admiral Antonio Barceló was based at the anchorage off Algeciras, across the bay from Gibraltar; its aim was to cut the supplies reaching the Rock from the African shore.
Spanish lookouts and gunboats were stationed at Cabrita Point (Punta Carnero), the western horn of the bay, to signal and intercept ships entering from the Strait.
Rodney's relief fleet put to sea from England on 27 December 1779.
On 16 January 1780 Rodney's fleet rounded Cape St Vincent.
Darby's relief fleet sailed in March 1781 — 13 March from St Helens/Spithead by the British count; the Spanish naval historian puts the sailing six days after 22 March.

Darby went first to the coast of Ireland to pick up victuallers from Cork, then made for Gibraltar, passing Cape St Vincent and bringing-to off Cape Spartel on the evening of 11 April 1781 before entering the bay on the 12th.
Howe's relief expedition sailed from Spithead on 11 September 1782.

Howe was off Cape St Vincent on 8 October 1782, entered the Strait on 11 October, but most transports missed the bay and were carried east into the Mediterranean; on 13 October the fleet lay off the Spanish coast near Fuengirola–Marbella before working back to land the stores (18 October).
Fort St Philip on Minorca hoisted the white flag on 4 February 1782; the capitulation was agreed and the garrison marched out on 5 February 1782, and the island passed to Spain.

Rodney's relief: news on arrival that on 8 Jan 1780 Rodney captured a Caracas Company convoy; convoy reached Gibraltar the night of ~18 Jan 1780 after defeating Langara (Moonlight Battle, 16 Jan); 21 sail of the line.
Darby's relief fleet sighted at daybreak 12 April 1781; stores landed in nine or ten days.

Howe's relief: on the evening of (implied) 11 Oct 1782 the Latona reported Howe's fleet of 34 sail of the line, 6 frigates, 31 ordnance transports and over 1,600 troops; most transports were swept into the Mediterranean; 25th and 59th Regiments landed on 18 Oct 1782.
